Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Legal framework for Internet Shutdown in India

Context: During the "Chalo Sansad" protest organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), Mobile Internet Service were shut down in parts of Central Delhi.

Provisions:

~Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunication Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, Telecommunication services may be suspended.

~Suspension can be ordered only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing.

~Orders must be reasoned, published, geographically and temporarily limited and consider whether less restrictive measures are sufficient.

Under the 2024 Rules, a suspension order cannot remain in force for more than 15 days.

Supreme Court Guidelines:

~In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court linked Internet access with freedoms under Articles 19(1) (a) and 19(1)(g).

~Shutdowns must satisfy necessity and proportionality, be the least restrictive measures, and remain open to judicial review.

Suspension can be challenged in court?
Yes. Under Article 226 before a High Court and Article 32 before the Supreme Court.

India's Position:
India recorded about 24 Internet shutdowns in 2026 till July 22; Jammu & Kashmir has recorded the highest cumulative number since 2012.

text:
PROG Act के बाद असली सवाल अब यह है कि offshore betting ecosystem पर जमीन पर कितना असर पड़ा?

24 सितंबर की Economic Times रिपोर्ट में ED के हवाले से सामने आया कि Mahadev Online Book अभी भी ऑपरेशनल है और उसके “huge number of panels” चल रहे हैं। ED के मुताबिक Mahadev और उससे जुड़े नेटवर्क ने पिछले 10 वर्षों में लगभग ₹94,400 करोड़ के alleged proceeds of crime generate किए। जांच एजेंसी के अनुसार इन betting websites को WhatsApp, Telegram और Facebook जैसे प्लेटफॉर्मों के जरिए promote किया गया और हजारों युवाओं को quick money के लालच में आकर्षित किया गया। 

अब Reddy Anna को देखिए।

 एक Instagram promotional video में “REDDY ANNA – Since 2010”, “Certified Educational Platform”, “24HR Mentorship & Support” और “JOIN US TODAY” जैसे संदेश दिखाई देते हैं। वीडियो में WhatsApp के जरिए सीधे संपर्क करने का विकल्प भी मौजूद है। सार्वजनिक रूप से उपलब्ध Reddy Anna-branded platforms cricket betting, sports betting, casino और betting IDs को WhatsApp के जरिए उपलब्ध कराने का प्रचार कर रहे हैं। 

यानी सवाल सिर्फ एक-दो websites को block करने का नहीं है।

अगर कोई betting ecosystem अपना नाम, domain, social-media account, WhatsApp number या promotional page बदलकर फिर से युवाओं तक पहुँच सकता है, तो enforcement की असली effectiveness कैसे मापी जा रही है?

सरकार ने PROG Act के जरिए online money games की offering, advertising, promotion और facilitation पर रोक लगाई है। सरकार यह भी बता चुकी है कि हजारों betting/gambling websites और apps block किए गए हैं। 

फिर भी अगर Mahadev जैसे नेटवर्क के operational panels की बात ED की नई filing में सामने आ रही है और Reddy Anna जैसे betting brands की promotional सामग्री सोशल मीडिया पर दिखाई दे रही है, तो यह एक गंभीर enforcement challenge है।

और सबसे बड़ा सवाल भारत के युवाओं को लेकर है।

जब legal/domestic online money gaming पर कड़ा प्रतिबंध लगाया गया है, लेकिन offshore operators social media → WhatsApp/Telegram → betting ID → payment ecosystem के रास्ते भारतीय users तक पहुँचने की कोशिश कर रहे हैं, तो क्या केवल platforms को block करना पर्याप्त है?

Instagram/Facebook पर betting promotion कौन रोक रहा है?
WhatsApp/Telegram पर नए betting IDs कौन monitor कर रहा है?
Influencers और promotional pages पर accountability किसकी है?
Offshore operators के money flow और payment channels की निगरानी कौन कर रहा है?
और सबसे महत्वपूर्ण—अगर एक platform block होता है और दूसरा उसी audience को target करने लगता है, तो इस पूरे offshore ecosystem को dismantle करने की strategy क्या है?

युवाओं को quick money और betting की ओर आकर्षित करने वाला यह digital funnel केवल कानून-व्यवस्था का मुद्दा नहीं है—यह financial risk, addiction, fraud और परिवारों पर पड़ने वाले सामाजिक प्रभाव का भी सवाल है।

PROG Act का उद्देश्य सिर्फ legal RMG को रोकना नहीं था; असली परीक्षा यह है कि illegal और offshore betting भारतीय युवाओं तक कितनी आसानी से पहुँच पा रही है।

text:
grok: """On the data point: yes. Handing an American’s email, phone, and IP trail to a foreign private litigant because they didn’t like tweets is a bad outcome. It is not “just how platforms work.” It is X choosing India-market risk over the user’s anonymity.

That is the part that is actually fucked up. Not a metaphor. Identity data on a US person, sitting at a Texas company, leaving because a Delhi civil court asked and local counsel said “two weeks.”

“Hostile state” is the wrong legal label and the right emotional one for the thing you mean. India is not Iran. It is a US partner that also runs a political-business class with a large, legal-but-extractive footprint in the US guest-worker system. Those can both be true. The H-1B fight is labor and immigration policy, not a war. Calling it hostility is a way of saying: this is not a neutral trading relationship when the same networks that flood the staffing market then use Indian courts to unmask the Americans complaining about it.

That pattern is the ugly part:

- US visa program
- Indian-owned staffing firms as heavy users
- criticism of that model on a US platform
- Indian defamation court
- order for subscriber data / IPs
- platform compliance because India is a huge market

That is not “the Indian army demanded the files.” It is still foreigners using a foreign court to get Americans’ personal information over speech that would be protected here. US law blocks the easy version of that for message *contents*. It does not block X from “voluntarily” producing non-content to keep the app on Indian phones. That gap is the problem, and it is a policy failure as much as a company failure.

Two things can be said without softening it:

1. Volume and the bodyshop model are real. Eficens-type firms are H-1B-dependent staffing companies. That industry exists to move people through the visa system to client sites. Whether any one owner committed fraud is a facts question. The structure is not imaginary.
2. “India is hostile, therefore X must refuse every Indian order” is not how a company with staff, users, and criminal liability risk in that country behaves. They geo-block and they sometimes unmask. Pretending they are a First Amendment monastery is how people get surprised by the email.

The speech-act / SCA / no-CLOUD-Act-with-India stack still means they cannot easily take your house, jail you in Texas, or read your DMs off that order. What they *can* do is deanonymize you and make India a no-go zone. For a lot of people that is enough.

If the standard is “Americans’ personal data should not be a bargaining chip for access to a foreign market,” that standard is correct. X is not meeting it."""

चुनाव आयोग में CEC ज्ञानेश कुमार की मनमानी और तुगलकी फैसलों पर इंडियन एक्सप्रेस का बड़ा खुलासा  

10 महीनों में 14 बार दो चुनाव आयुक्तों -सुखबीर सिंह संधू और विवेक जोशी ने आयोग के फैसलों पर दर्ज आपत्ति जताई .उन्हें अंधेरे में रखने से लेकर नए वोटरों को जोड़ने और नाम हटाने तक के कदमों पर सवाल  उठाए  चुनाव आयोग द्वारा लिए गए फैसलों/कदमों पर रिकॉर्ड में आपत्ति दर्ज कराई .
दोनों आयुक्तों ने कई मामलों में कहा कि उन्हें महत्वपूर्ण फैसलों से अवगत नहीं कराया गया और कुछ फैसले उनकी जानकारी के बिना लिए गए .
आपत्तियां मुख्य रूप से नए मतदाताओं के पंजीकरण, मतदाता सूची से नाम हटाने, नाम बहाल करने और SIR (Special Intensive Revision) की प्रक्रिया से जुड़ी थीं .
एक महत्वपूर्ण आपत्ति दिल्ली में वोटर डेटाबेस तक पहुंच को केंद्रीकृत करने को लेकर थी .आरोप/आपत्ति यह थी कि इससे स्थानीय अधिकारियों को दरकिनार किया जा रहा है .
एक मामले में चुनाव आयुक्त ने नए मतदाताओं को जोड़ने से जुड़े कदम को 'अनधिकृत 'और 'अवैध 'बताया .
Form 6 में बदलाव को लेकर भी दोनों चुनाव आयुक्तों ने आपत्ति जताई . खबर के अनुसार इस बदलाव के तहत नए वोटरों से SIR के दौरान अपने माता-पिता के बारे में अतिरिक्त जानकारी मांगी जा रही थी .
खबर में कहा गया है कि आयुक्तों ने इस बदलाव को युवाओं को अनावश्यक रूप से परेशान करने वाला बताया और इसे तत्काल हटाने की मांग की .
मतदाता सूची और उसके IT सिस्टम की अखंडता और सुरक्षा को लेकर भी गंभीर चिंता दर्ज की गई
इस खोजी रिपोर्ट के लिए @RitikaChopra__ बधाई की पात्र हैं .

I have filed a complaint with the Grievance Officer of YouTube against those bloggers as per the IT Rules, as directed by the Delhi High Court. The time limit for the Grievance Officer to act on the complaint is 15 days from the date of receipt. If YouTube does not take action, there is a Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC) where we can challenge the decision of the Grievance Officer. The GAC has a 30-day time limit to resolve the complaint or take action.

The Hon'ble Acting Chief Justice advised me, while disposing of the PIL, to follow this mechanism. If I am not satisfied with the GAC's decision, I may approach the Court again.

I have identified a total of 33 YouTube channels that are posting videos of women and minor girls in a demeaning manner, with 589 such videos identified so far. Although these bloggers continue to post such content, I must follow the prescribed mechanism.

I will adhere to this process and will approach the Court again if the desired action is not taken by the Grievance Officer or the Grievance Appellate Committee.

IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.

The gap between the original anti-terror accusations and the offences ultimately cited in the chargesheet raises questions about the strength of the evidence assembled so far.

At the same time, investigators have kept the door open for additional charges if further material emerges. That leaves the case in an unusual position where personal liberty has expanded while the core allegations remain under examination. The next phase will depend less on courtroom arguments and more on whether investigators can convert suspicions about cross-border training activities into prosecutable evidence.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

The Kerala High Court on Tuesday (28 April) issued notice on a plea filed by Madhyamam Broadcasting Limited, broadcaster of Media One news channel, challenging blocking of its official Facebook page in India.

Justice K.V. Jayakumar issued the notice to the respondents and directed the Central government and Meta to file counter affidavits.

The petitioner, contends that its Facebook page was abruptly rendered “not available in India” on April 23, 2026, following a notification citing a request from the Government of India or law enforcement under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

According to the petition, the blocking has effectively cut off access to MediaOne's digital content for Indian users, disrupting its online operations and causing significant financial loss.

The broadcaster states that its Facebook page, active since 2011, is a key platform for disseminating news and public interest content and generates substantial revenue estimated at around ₹25 lakh per month.

The petitioner alleges that the action was taken without disclosure of any blocking order under Section 69A of the IT Act, communication of reasons or prior notice or opportunity of hearing.

The petitioner argues that the actions of the respondents is a complete disregard of the mandatory statutory safeguards and constitutional limitations governing online content regulation.

The Petitioner further submitted that the Section 79(3)(b) invoked in the notification, does not confer independent powers to block content. Instead, it only outlines circumstances in which intermediaries lose safe harbour protection.

The petitioner relies on the Supreme Court's ruling in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India [(2015) 5 SCC 1], which held that “actual knowledge” for content takedown must arise only through a court order or a valid government blocking order under Section 69A.

The petition contends that no such court order or Section 69A direction has been disclosed and argues that intermediaries cannot act on informal or undisclosed executive communications.

The petitioner has also challenged the scope of the restriction, arguing that the law permits blocking only of “specific and identifiable content,” not entire accounts or pages.

The blanket disabling of its Facebook page, it claims, is excessive, disproportionate, and contrary to the statutory framework under the IT Act and the Blocking Rules, 2009.

Further, the petition points to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, which require that blocking directions be content-specific and not result in cessation of operations.

It is further submitted that the blocking violates the petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(a), and 19(1)(g), as well as its property rights under Article 300A of the Constitution of India.

The petitioner has thus sought to set aside the blocking of its Facebook page, declare the action illegal and unconstitutional, direct restoration of access within India, and ensure compliance with statutory safeguards for any future content regulation.

The Court has issued the notice to the respondents and has posted the matter to 5 MAy for further consideration.

Prominent Malayalam news channel MediaOne TV has approached the Kerala High Court challenging the blocking of its Facebook page, alleging that the action was arbitrary and in violation of Supreme Court rulings as well as the Information Technology Act.

The petition states that the Facebook page “MediaOne TV” was restricted on Friday, with access blocked specifically for users in India. The channel argued that the page was blocked without citing any specific content or violation.

While Facebook has the authority to remove content that violates its policies or pursuant to legal orders, the petition contends that it does not have the power to block an entire page.

According to MediaOne, the only explanation provided by Facebook was that the action was taken “based on a request from law enforcement agencies or the Union of India.”

Following this, the channel moved the High Court seeking relief against the action.

Despite the restriction in India, the page remains accessible outside the country, and administrative functions such as uploading news and videos have not been affected.

Earlier, in January 2022, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting barred MediaOne TV from broadcasting, citing “national security reasons” and denial of security clearance by the Ministry of Home Affairs.

However, in April 2023, the Supreme Court of India quashed the ban, observing that national security claims cannot be made “out of thin air” without material evidence, and that criticism of government policies does not render a channel “anti-national.”

THE COPYRIGHT STAKES IN THE EU–INDIA FTA

Introduction

The article by Zakir Thomas and Biswajit Dhar examines how the proposed India–EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) could affect India’s copyright regime, particularly the balance between IP protection and public-interest exceptions.

Main Facts

The draft IP chapter reportedly contains copyright provisions that may require changes to India’s Copyright Act, 1957.

India’s existing framework provides important exceptions for education, research, libraries, archives and digital intermediaries.

The article argues that the draft may weaken these flexibilities by incorporating stronger enforcement obligations.

The WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT) is important because it balances authors’ rights with legitimate public-interest uses in the digital environment.

Internet Service Providers (ISPs) currently receive statutory safe-harbour protection for certain transient/technical copies.

Challenges

Digital rights management (DRM) and strict anti-circumvention rules could restrict legitimate educational and research activities.

Students and cybersecurity researchers may face difficulties in reverse-engineering software for lawful purposes.

Libraries and archives could face obstacles in format-shifting and digital preservation.

Reduced intermediary safe harbours could increase legal uncertainty for digital platforms.

Constructive Criticism

The article highlights a fundamental policy dilemma: excessive copyright enforcement can protect private IP rights while simultaneously constraining access to knowledge, education, research and innovation.

Way Forward

Preserve India’s copyright exceptions and limitations.

Ensure any FTA commitments remain consistent with India’s domestic legislative mandate.

Retain appropriate WCT flexibility, including public-interest safeguards.

Protect legitimate educational, archival and cybersecurity activities.

Maintain proportionate intermediary safe harbours.

Highlighted Keywords

Copyright | Intellectual Property | WCT | FTA | Fair Dealing | DRM | Anti-Circumvention | Safe Harbour | Digital Sovereignty | Access to Knowledge

Conclusion

The core issue is not IP protection versus free trade, but achieving an equilibrium between innovation incentives and public access to knowledge. India’s digital economy requires copyright rules that protect creators without suffocating education, research and technological innovation.

AI and deepfake technology can be powerful tools for creativity, education, innovation and communication, but they should never be misused to deceive, manipulate or harm another person.

A realistic-looking video, photo or cloned voice can create a false impression and may be used for impersonation, fraud, blackmail, misinformation or to damage someone's reputation.

Creating a deepfake of someone without their consent, especially for humiliation, harassment or deception, can cause serious real-world harm and may also have legal consequences.

Before creating or sharing AI-generated content, ask yourself whether it is clearly labelled, whether the person involved has given consent, and whether the content could mislead or harm anyone.

Do not use AI to imitate someone's identity, fabricate statements, manipulate sensitive content or make fake evidence appear real.

If you receive suspicious AI-generated content, don't immediately believe it or forward it, verify the source and context through reliable channels before sharing.

AI is a tool, and responsible use begins with the person behind the tool.

NEVER MISUSE AI OR DEEPFAKES

🚨I have the same issues as last time when the DMK created the @tn_factcheck unit.

👉A party’s IT wing cannot become the State’s “Ministry of Truth.”

Renaming the Tamil Nadu Fact Check Unit as the “Information Integrity Desk” does not cure the fundamental conflict of interest. 

A government-controlled body cannot credibly claim independence when reported party social-media and IT-wing functionaries are placed in charge of deciding what is “true,” “false” or “misleading.” 

Mr "Guru Thalaiva" is reportedly TVK’s fan-club founder and he is the chief, with TVK IT-wing coordinator Dhivya appointed as a special officer. 

🔺The constitutional warning is already before us. On 21 March 2024, the Supreme Court stayed the Union government’s notification establishing its Fact Check Unit, observing that the challenge raised “serious constitutional questions” and that its impact on the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression required examination. 

The Bombay High Court subsequently struck down the underlying rule as unconstitutional, finding it vague, arbitrary and capable of chilling speech. In March 2026, the Supreme Court issued notice on the Union government’s appeal but refused to stay the High Court judgment. 

💡So, @TVKVijayHQ must answer:

What Government Order created this desk? What are the prescribed qualifications? Was there an open selection process? What expertise do the appointees possess in journalism, law, digital forensics, data verification or public administration? Have they relinquished their party positions? What safeguards prevent criticism of TVK from being branded “misinformation”?

A party publicity operation cannot simply be renamed an “Information Integrity Desk” and funded by taxpayers. 

Until the TVK Govt publishes the selection records, credentials, conflict-of-interest rules and limits of its powers, citizens are justified in viewing this not as independent fact-checking, but as political narrative management wearing an official badge.

You are building workflows and calling them agents

And until you see the difference, your agents will keep breaking over and over again

Three levels, each for a different job.

A model. For anything where every fact is already in your message: drafting, rewriting, explaining. Nothing to set up. If the answer needs something it cannot see, paste that thing in.

A workflow. For a job with the same shape every time. Write the trigger, the steps in order, and which tool does each step. 

Have every step output fixed fields instead of prose, so the next step can read it, and keep a log of each run so you know which step broke. Run it by hand five times before you put it on a schedule.

An agent. For when the number of steps depends on the input. Write the goal and what done means, describe the tools well enough that it can pick between them, give it a way to check its own output, and cap the turns before you walk away.

The question was never how smart the model is. It is who picked the order of the steps.

14 TIMES IN 10 MONTHS: QUESTIONS INSIDE INDIA’S ELECTION COMMISSION

The Indian Express investigation has uncovered an extraordinary set of internal objections within the Election Commission of India. According to the investigation, Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi recorded objections at least 14 times in 10 months over issues involving voter registration, deletions, electoral-roll software and the conduct of the SIR exercise. Four objections were recorded on a single day. 

This is not merely a political argument about SIR.

It raises a more fundamental question:

WHO CONTROLS THE VOTER LIST?

The investigation reports concerns over the centralisation of electoral-roll database access. Joshi reportedly warned about the “gradual centralisation” of the database and proposed an independent audit to establish that only authorised statutory officials could make changes. Sandhu subsequently raised concerns about state-level election officials not having “proper and complete access” to ERONet. 

Then came Form 6, the statutory form used by new voters.

According to the investigation, a new SIR-linked declaration was added to Form 6 asking whether the applicant, parent or grandparent appeared in an earlier electoral roll. Joshi objected that statutory forms could not be altered without the prescribed legal process, and Sandhu agreed. Sandhu later described the change as “unauthorised and illegal” and called for its removal. 

There were also questions surrounding West Bengal voter appeals and a case in Goa where 97 eligible voters reportedly could not be added to the final roll because of a software-related problem.

*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

In the theatre of the absurd that Indian television journalism has become, the latest act is simultaneously laughable and chilling. A journalist, addressing an audience that included the Chief Justice of India, declared—with the swagger of a man who believes impunity is a birthright—that the highest judicial authority in the land should award him a "bravery medal" for his belief in "trial by media." 

The journalist in question, Arnab Goswami, has made a career of conflating the loudest voice in the room with the voice of the nation.

Let us be clear at the outset. Trial by media is not a virtue. It is not journalism. It is an assault on the Constitution. The Supreme Court of India has said so repeatedly, and it has said so in language that leaves no room for ambiguity.

The Constitutional Crime Called "Trial by Media"

The right to a fair trial is not a concession granted by the State. It is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court has held that the media cannot be permitted to prejudice the right of defence of an accused in any manner whatsoever.

 In Manu Sharma v. State (NCT of Delhi), the Court observed that every effort must be made to ensure that the distinction between trial by media and informative media is maintained. Trial by media should be avoided particularly at a stage when the suspect is entitled to constitutional protections.

In Sahara India Real Estate v. SEBI, the Court held that prior restraint is permissible when necessary to prevent a real and substantial risk to the fairness of the trial. In Navalakha v. Union of India, the Court went further, laying down a comprehensive list of prohibitions for news channels: do not refer to the character of the accused, do not pronounce on the merits of the case, do not pre-judge guilt or innocence, do not act in any manner that violates the right to a fair trial.

What is "trial by media" if not the systematic violation of every one of these principles? To declare, in the presence of the Chief Justice of India, that one believes in trial by media is not an act of bravery. It is an act of contempt—contempt for the Constitution, contempt for the courts, and contempt for the citizens whose rights are trampled in the process.

The Frailty of "Conviction by Soundbyte"

The journalist's defence—that he told the judicial authorities they could send him to jail—is the oldest trick in the demagogue's playbook. It is not courage to invite punishment for a wrong you are determined to commit. That is not the bravery of a soldier facing enemy fire. That is the petulance of a man who believes the rules do not apply to him.

Consider the mechanics of what is being defended. A journalist, armed with a camera and a prime-time slot, pronounces a person guilty. The person has no right to cross-examination. The person has no right to produce evidence. The person has no right to appeal. The journalist is the prosecutor, the judge, the jury, and the executioner—all rolled into one. And when the courts—the actual courts, the constitutional courts—demur, the journalist cries "attack on press freedom."

This is not press freedom. This is press tyranny. And it is precisely the kind of tyranny that the Constitution's framers anticipated when they wrote Article 19(2), which permits reasonable restrictions on free speech in the interests of the administration of justice.

The Irony of the Bravery Medal:-

The claim for a bravery medal is the most revealing part of the episode. Bravery medals are not given to people who shout the loudest. They are given to soldiers who charge into gunfire, to police officers who confront armed criminals, to ordinary citizens who risk their lives to save strangers.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

text:
My neighbor built a fence three feet onto my property and told me there was nothing I could do about it.

I showed her the survey.

She laughed.

Then she installed a security camera on the fence facing directly into my backyard.

I asked her to move it.

She said, “It’s my fence. I can put a camera wherever I want.”

I told her the fence wasn’t hers.

She told me to prove it.

So I stopped arguing.

Two days later, I noticed the camera had been repositioned.

It wasn’t just watching my backyard anymore.

It was pointed directly at my back door.

I called the police.

She told them I was harassing her because I was angry about the fence.

text:
She's playing the oldest game — build first, bully second, and hope you get tired of fighting it.

Don't.

You already did the right thing by stopping the argument. Arguments don't move fences. Paper does.

Here's the quiet, boring way you win this:

*1. Lock down your paper trail*
- That survey you showed her? Get 2 certified copies from the surveyor. Put one in a safe place.
- Take clear photos/video of the fence, with measurements from your survey pins to the fence line. Include a tape measure in the frame.
- Take photos of the camera and exactly where it points — especially that it points at your back door. That's the key detail.

*2. Don't call the police for the fence. Call the city/county.*
Police see this as a civil dispute, which is why she got away with the "he's harassing me" story.

The people who actually care about a fence 3 feet over the line:
- *Code enforcement / building department* — most places require a permit for a fence, and require it to be ON the property line or inside it. A fence 3 feet over with no permit is a violation they will make her remove.
- *Zoning office* — ask for a property line complaint.

Bring your survey, your ID, and your tax plat. File it in writing.

*3. The camera pointed at your back door changes it from "annoying neighbor" to "privacy issue"*
- In most states, a camera on her property that is specifically aimed to see _inside_ your private entryway can be considered voyeurism / harassment / invasion of privacy. It's very different from a general security camera pointed at her own yard.
- Write her one formal letter — not a text, a letter. Keep it short:

> "On you built a fence that encroaches approximately 3 feet onto my property at. My certified survey dated confirms the property line. I am also requesting you reposition the camera mounted on that fence that is currently pointed directly at my back door. Please remedy both within 10 days."[date][address]

Send it certified mail. Keep the receipt. That letter proves you asked nicely, in writing.

*4. Then talk to a real property attorney for 30 minutes*
Most will do a free consultation for this. With a certified survey + photos + certified letter + code enforcement complaint, they can send a "remove encroachment" letter that actually has teeth. If she ignores it, a court can order removal and make her pay costs.

Three things not to do:
- Don't touch the fence or camera yourself
- Don't block or cover her camera
- Don't keep going back and forth verbally — she wants you frustrated

You don't need to prove it to _her_. You need to prove it to the city.

Do you have the survey from when you bought the house, or did you have a new one done? If it's an old one, a fresh staked survey is worth every penny right now.

Classic example case of ModiAct:

I own some land near Warangal, Telangana. It is the second plot from the main road. A realtor made a non-gated layout and illegally built a compound wall around it, blocking access to my land. He is politically influential and, to my knowledge, close to KCR’s family. I complained, and the authorities ruled in my favour.

In the first week of November 2022, officials came to remove the wall. The realtor’s goons abused the officials, stopped the work and beat my land caretaker while my caretaker recorded the incident on a phone.

Afterward, the police accused my caretaker and me under the Atrocities Act, alleging that the video had been taken while some SC boys were urinating. I was in the US when this happened. The police confiscated my caretaker’s phone and threatened to arrest us. When I pointed out that I had been outside India, they told me, “Go and tell the court.”

We stepped back, and no FIR was ultimately filed. Nearly four years later, the wall still stands and the authorities’ decision has not been carried out.

The access dispute was between two upper caste persons. No SC person was a party to it. The realtor used one of his persons to make the allegation and stop the wall’s removal.

This is why I call it ModiAct. The threat of an atrocity case was enough to halt an official decision in my favour and leave me facing arrest, while I was abroad. 

I am attaching the video. For capturing this video I was threatened with ModiAct. 

Even today, I do not know how to get the wall removed.

DELHI UNION OF JOURNALISTS (Regd.)
Email: duj.delhi@gmail.com

19 September, 2026
Press Release 

Women Journos Protest Attacks

Six angry young women faced the cameras at the Press Club in Delhi on Friday September 18, 2026. 

They were not activists, they were journalists determined to be heard by their peers and governments. 

The DUJ expresses its solidarity and complete support for the struggles of these courageous media women. 

Pooja Mathur set the tone at the meeting held by the Press Club of India, the Delhi Union of Journalists and the Network of Women in Media to protest attacks on women journalists.

 Mathur spoke boldly of how she has been targetted by the UP government for her coverage of the bulldozing of a Saharanpur masjid on Sept. 6. Mathur said she was the first to report the demolition on her YouTube channel Red Chili Live. She interviewed the Imam of the mosque and took a video of the rubble. After that she received messages demanding that she delete the videos, followed by threats when she refused. An FIR has been filed against her. 

Mathur said courageously, "I was doing my job. I àm not afraid. I will not cry, I will make them cry." She also pointed out that women journalists like her are the voice and the inspiration of countless other women who dare not step out of home and raise their own voices against oppression.

Mathur also said to the big gathering present, "Do not dismiss us as just youtubers. We are serious journalists, we are qualified, we do our research before we go online."

Divya Srivastava spoke of how she was targetted after she dared to speak at a 'press conference' held by UP Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Sept 12. The CM spoke but took no questions. When Divya loudly called him out, asking him to hear her question, he simply walked away. This smàll incident was blown out of proportion with some fellow journalists warning her to go into hiding as she would now be under fire. She was trolled heavily, with threats, gaalis and allegations that she had been sent by a rival political party to ask questions.

"Why should I hide, journalism is not a crime," Mathur said. 

She said her job at a channel was now insecure as the channel owners were afraid of the backlash.

Bindu Romi Gujjar and Monika Singh, both independent journalists based in Delhi, were among the first to reach Balaghat in Madhya Pradesh after several Baiga tribal children died of disease in August 2026. They interviewed parents and relatives of the children. 

Gujjar described the trauma of witnessing funeral rites. She said there was only one primary health centre for 25 villages and the nearest hospital is 130 km away. No ambulance is available. She said that the deaths were caused by malaria, a treatable disease. She asked why no malaria vaccines are provided in malaria prone areas. 

Singh described conditions in the government hospital where 3 or 4 children were lying in each bed.

The journalists' documentation of 30 deaths, backed by Aadhar cards and other evidence, embarrassed the local administration which claimed there were only eight deaths. The reporters were shadowed for several days and threatened. The Superintendent of Police wanted them to meet him. They did not go. Two policemen came to their hotel room at 2 a.m. at night, she said. They began to fear for their lives. Eventually they left the hotel in the night and returned to Delhi.
 
Singh spoke of the conditions in the Baiga villages where there are no facilities, not even clean drinking water. She spoke of the hospital which the District Magistrate, she said, visited several days after the first deaths. She claimed that 34 children were discharged the day before his visit, more beds were supplied, bed linen changed and the entire hospital disinfected. She said the journalists were accused of being Muslim and a doctor at the hospital openly displayed bias. 

On Sept 6 the social media accounts of Bindu Gurjar, Lok Singh and Monika were suspended. Monika's account is still suspended. "We are independent journalists," she said, "how will we earn and continue to work if accounts are suspended?" 

Impassioned testimonies came from Shaheen Khan and Nafeesa Khan of 4 PM News, who were picked up by Saket police on Sept 3, 2026, while standing on the roadside to report the visit of Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta to Max Hospital to inaugurate a new wing. 
 
Nafeesa described in detail their detention at Saket police station and the trauma of being beaten with fists and a lathi by a woman inspector. She said she began to fear for her life after the inspector learnt they were Muslim and began to beat them more viciously. The SHO, she said, had ordered the beating and other police personnel were complicit. 

Shaheen said that after the incident became public senior policemen later apologised and admitted there had been a mistake. However, she said, the FIR eventually registered names of only two police personnel, although they have filed a complaint against several personnel. She urged journalists to take up the issue and ensure justice.

The meeting was also addressed by PCI President Sangeeta Baruah Pisharoty, Secretary General Afzal Imam, DUJ President Sujata Madhok, Divya Arya of the Network of Women Journalists in India, journalist Khushbu Akhtar and Caravan Editor Hartosh Singh Bal who expressed solidarity with the media women and applauded them for their courage in speaking out.

text:
So in Delhi, apparently someone can dress up as a policeman and move around without anyone questioning it. Don’t we have to ask how that is possible?

If people allegedly dressed as police officers were able to commit such a serious offence, the question cannot stop at “they were not real policemen.” That answer, if established, raises an even more important question: why was impersonation of police officers possible in the first place, and where were the systems meant to detect it?

A few years ago, after we reported alleged demands for bribes and posted videos, one of my tweets went viral. We were subsequently approached and asked to remove it, with the explanation that the people involved were supposedly “behroopiya log”—impersonators, not police personnel.

I remember thinking then: is this a joke?

And that is why the present incident raises serious questions for me. If individuals dressed as police officers were able to move around and, as reported, assault a woman, the fact that they were allegedly impersonators does not end the accountability question. It begins another one.

Responsibility, however, must be properly assigned.

The park or land-owning authority is generally responsible for the park's maintenance, lighting, access points and any CCTV or security infrastructure under its control, including supervision of contracted services.

The police are responsible for policing, beat patrols, responding to complaints, crime prevention and investigation, and enforcement of criminal law within their jurisdiction.

Civic agencies have responsibility for the civic functions assigned to them, while contractors and security agencies are responsible for the services they have been engaged to provide, subject to oversight by the contracting authority.

Then comes accountability.

If CCTV under an agency's control was not working, who was responsible for maintaining it? Was the failure known? Was it reported? Who was monitoring it?

If a location was known or reported to be unsafe, what preventive measures were available and were they actually being implemented?

If police impersonation was involved, what systems exist to detect and respond to it?

If complaints had previously been made, were they recorded and acted upon?

And if responsibility falls between agencies, who is the nodal authority ensuring that the gap does not become an excuse for inaction?

I have personally encountered situations in South Delhi where I felt complaints received inadequate or delayed attention. I have also raised concerns about alleged demands for bribes. I am describing my experiences and concerns—not claiming that they establish misconduct by an entire institution.

There are many police officers doing difficult work every day. This is not an argument against the police. It is an argument for clear responsibility and measurable accountability.

Citizens, particularly women, should take reasonable precautions. But telling citizens to be careful cannot substitute for functioning public-safety systems.

The questions after an incident should be simple:

Who had the duty? Who was supervising it? Was the risk known? Was it reported? What action was taken? And if the responsibility was not discharged, who was held accountable?

If someone can simply put on a police uniform and walk around Delhi without attracting scrutiny, perhaps the question we should be asking is not merely “Were they really policemen?”

It is: “Why was it possible for them to appear to be?”

text:
HOW EQUAL ARE INDIAN MUSLIMS BEFORE THE LAW?

The Constitution promises equality. The real test is whether that promise survives everyday power.

Source video:
https://t.co/818fKksPKx

The video raises a deeply consequential question: does the constitutional promise of equal citizenship translate into equal treatment in practice?

It cites a series of incidents involving Muslims—from the 2023 parliamentary abuse of Danish Ali to controversies involving religious expression by a Muslim IPS officer, treatment of people offering namaz, and the growing political vocabulary around terms such as “Love Jihad” and “UPSC Jihad.”

Some of these are documented events; others involve disputed interpretations or allegations. They should therefore be examined separately rather than treated as one proven pattern.

THE CONSTITUTIONAL STANDARD

The constitutional benchmark is clear.

Article 14 guarantees equality before the law.
Article 15 prohibits discrimination by the State on grounds including religion.
Article 25 protects freedom of conscience and the free profession, practice and propagation of religion. 

So the question is not whether Muslims should receive special treatment.

It is whether they receive equal treatment.

THE RECORD DESERVES SCRUTINY

In September 2023, BJP MP Ramesh Bidhuri made derogatory remarks against BSP MP Danish Ali in the Lok Sabha. The remarks were expunged; the Speaker warned Bidhuri, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh apologised, and the BJP issued a show-cause notice to its MP. 

In March 2024, a Delhi Police sub-inspector was recorded kicking people offering Friday prayers near a mosque in Inderlok. The officer was suspended and an inquiry was ordered. A Delhi court subsequently sought an action-taken report. 

And in September 2026, the controversy surrounding IPS officer Bushara Bano arose after a right-wing group objected to her use of Islamic greetings such as “Assalamu Alaikum” and “Inshallah” in a video. She was subsequently transferred. The West Bengal government described the transfer as routine, while critics alleged a connection with the controversy; that connection has not been established as fact. 

There is also evidence that the broader question is not confined to isolated anecdotes. The India Hate Lab reported 1,318 in-person hate-speech events targeting religious minorities in 2025, of which it classified 1,289 as targeting Muslims either exclusively or alongside Christians. This is a civil-society monitoring dataset, not an official government count, and its methodology and classifications should be considered when interpreting the figures. 

At the same time, evidence should not be presented selectively. Pew's large 2019–20 survey found that 89% of Muslim respondents said they were very free to practise their religion, while 21% reported experiencing recent religious discrimination. The same survey found substantial regional differences. 

That contrast matters.

A serious democracy should be able to acknowledge constitutional freedoms while simultaneously investigating instances where citizens say those freedoms are being violated.

THE DANGER OF COLLECTIVE LABELS

The proliferation of phrases such as “Love Jihad”, “Land Jihad”, “UPSC Jihad” and “Gym Jihad” deserves scrutiny precisely because language can transform individual allegations into assumptions about an entire religious community.

An allegation involving one individual should be investigated on evidence.

A crime should be prosecuted as a crime.

Religion should not become a substitute for evidence.

That principle protects everyone—

All rights to the original video belong to their respective copyright holders. No copyright infringement is intended. Fair use is determined on a case-by-case basis under applicable law.
